Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB414.xml). In Shanduo Zhenzai's section headed 'comments on old cases,' a story recounts Nengren Jizhou Hong sending a monk back to Huangbo, where the monk awakens. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB418.xml). At a New Year evening meeting Huiyue Xu quotes two old teachers, one saying New Year Buddha-Dharma is present and the other saying it is absent. He says both are caught by that opposition and that his own judgment deserves blows too. After a pause he announces a verse: its first two lines describe pines and morning clouds, and its closing couplet reuses Du Fu's orioles and egrets. Huiyue voices the lines in his current verse while drawing on the older poem.

Senses.Explanation: Du Fu's familiar spring landscape couplet becomes a Chan answer or cap where a teacher refuses to reduce the matter to an abstract explanation. The literary couplet comes from Du Fu. Yingning Zhijing answers a west-hall monk's request for a phrase beyond new and old teachings by giving the birds and willows directly, then continues the dialogue about royal and ministerial positions. In Shanduo Zhenzai's 'comments on old cases' section, a reported Nengren Jizhou Hong episode ends when a monk returns to Huangbo and awakens; the unintroduced couplet immediately after the story is Shanduo's capping line in that genre, not speech attributed to Nengren. Huiyue Xu incorporates the same two lines as the close of his own four-line New Year verse after rebuking the old opposition of having or lacking New Year Buddha-Dharma. The three records show present Chan uses of one older poem, not three original compositions of the landscape line.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1986B.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Liangjie of Dongshan, Ruizhou preserves Dongshan Liangjie's five-position verse. Under arrival within both, he says not to avoid crossing blades, then compares a skilled hand to a lotus blooming in fire with a drive to soar upward. Occurrences.Kwic: 兼中至，兩刃交鋒不須避。好手猶如火裏蓮，宛然自有冲天志。兼中至就，功位齊彰時立。正既來偏，偏必兼正。作家相見之際，明暗交參，縱奪互用，不涉一毫擬議，自然不至傷鋒犯手，如火裏蓮花，而卒無所損也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1437.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian quotes Dongshan Liangjie's line while explaining the five positions. Yongjue says arrival within both is where action and position appear together: when capable practitioners meet, light and dark intersect, taking and granting operate without deliberation, and neither blade harms the hand. He uses the lotus in fire to describe that unharmed response. The verse itself remains Dongshan's, while the account of how crossing blades works is Yongjue's own interpretive use. This row therefore adds commentary rather than a second origin for the saying.

Senses.Explanation: The two halls disputing over the cat names the public case in which the eastern and western halls quarrel, Nanquan demands a word that will save the cat, and the assembly does not answer. The early Zutang Ji supplies a cause omitted by almost every later version: Nanquan’s chief seat kept a cat, the neighboring berth or its occupant suffered damage to a leg or foot, and a quarrel arose. The terse phrase “the neighboring berth or its occupant suffered damage to a leg or foot” (鄰床損腳) does not decide between damaged furniture and an injured person or explain how the damage happened. The Wumenguan instead has the eastern and western halls disputing and gives no cause. Much later, Liangting Jingting retells another origin: one hall leader says the precepts do not permit keeping cats and dogs, while the other wants the cat retained to control mice. These are source-attributed layers of the case, not details that can be silently combined into one historical account.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the two halls fight over the cat
AlternateTargets: the two halls dispute the cat
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “the two halls fight over the cat.” The exact phrase occurs 30 times in 29 allowlisted texts; expanded forms specify “the east and west halls.” In the Chan record it is the opening formula and a short name for Nanquan's cat case. The monks of the two halls dispute a cat; Nanquan holds it up and says, “If you can speak, I will not cut it,” no one answers, and he cuts it. When Zhaozhou returns, Nanquan recounts the event; Zhaozhou puts a sandal on his head and leaves, and Nanquan says that had Zhaozhou been present, he would have saved the cat. Later records quote the formula before asking what should have been said, composing verses on the case, or giving prose comments. The exact headword names the dispute that occasions the case; it is not a separate event from “Nanquan cuts the cat.” Elsewhere the corpus explicitly asks why Nanquan cut the cat if killing living beings is a major precept, but no occurrence of this exact formula states Nanquan's reason.
Senses.Note: The explicit precept question belongs to the linked cat-cutting family and is anchored under “cut the cat” and “Nanquan cuts the cat”, whose headwords it contains. It is not duplicated here as a headword-free occurrence. The corpus alternates the two graphs for “cat” (貓) and often adds “east and west” (東西).

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉因兩堂爭貓，乃提起云：「道得即不斬。」眾無對，泉便斬之。趙州自外至，泉舉前話，州脫草履安頭上而出，泉云：「子若在，即救得貓兒也。」

Senses.Note: Four distinct current Tier2 appraisal families quote one old exclamation. Heshan Pu, also source-named Depu in the reserve biography, is the speaker; Huanglong Huinan is his interlocutor and the old man in the line. Pu remains source-named and unlinked, without confusing him with another roster Heshan. X70’s two exact hits are the old exclamation and its repetition within one continuous commentary, covered by one window and one family. X66’s different but unattributed collected verse is disclosed as reserve; X82/X83/X85 biographies add no new original event.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1376.xml). Chijue Daochong develops Pu's encounter as an example of deep doubt leading to deep awakening. Pu asks about Kashyapa's command to knock down the flagpole, but Huanglong asks about his brief stay at Yuquan and then bows his head. Pu rushes out with the selected exclamation. Chijue repeats it, saying argument and explanation have fallen away, and links flagpole, Yuquan and bowed head as one working. He then warns that even this is only a resting place and demands attention to what precedes teachers and schools. The two exact hits belong to this one sustained appraisal.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB236.xml). Lianyue Daozheng raises the case before his own community at Yuquan. He says Pu traveled without the eye for travel, missed the place where he should have relinquished himself and finally could not get past Huanglong's wall. Yet he credits Pu with recognizing what had happened and not betraying the teacher. Lianyue asks whether Huanglong answered Pu's question or not, then turns Pu's earlier rushed departure into an invitation for the present monks to stay and examine. The quotation serves a distinct place-specific teaching challenge.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB311.xml). Juelang Daosheng quotes Pu's question and exclamation but reverses the expected victory: he says Huanglong, who spent his life manipulating Buddha hands and donkey feet, was caught by this lecturer. His following verse moves from the famous difficulty of the Sichuan road to a barrier on level ground, warns against a false rooster and ends with the single spit leaving countless doors at ease. This independent critical reading keeps Pu as the old speaker while refusing to make his apparent surrender a simple final defeat.

Senses.Explanation: Pu's reputation as a formidable scriptural debater collapses before Huanglong's unelaborated bow of the head. His exclamation turns that reputation against himself: all the tiger's command of explanations is no match for the old teacher's least gesture. Later teachers read the encounter as a breakthrough through doubt, a challenge addressed to their own community or even a reversal in which the teacher is caught. Chijue Daochong develops Pu's encounter as an example of deep doubt leading to deep awakening. Pu asks about Kashyapa's command to knock down the flagpole, but Huanglong asks about his brief stay at Yuquan and then bows his head. Pu rushes out with the selected exclamation. Chijue repeats it, saying argument and explanation have fallen away, and links flagpole, Yuquan and bowed head as one working. He then warns that even this is only a resting place and demands attention to what precedes teachers and schools. The two exact hits belong to this one sustained appraisal. Senses.Explanation: To ‘hand over with both hands’ is to make a complete and formal transfer of something entrusted to another. Masters promise to hand over a staff if someone can answer, and other witnesses transfer the ancestral robe, the ancestral family estate, or a teaching charge before the assembly. Some occurrences are conditional challenges; others describe an accomplished transmission.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X67/X67n1310.xml). Picking Up Jewels from the Eight Directions Collection. Senses.Explanation: An old-case retort about misclassifying two parts becomes a reusable challenge to fixed divisions in Chan teaching. The Eight Directions collection presents Dazhu holding up a staff to a scripture lecturer and asking whether it is samadhi. When the lecturer has no answer, Fojian Huiqin speaks in his place with the cryptic line about two parts and the preceding category. Shuai'an Fanzong later ends a lively hall address by using the same line after reducing many sayings to one saying and many phrases to one phrase. Jieshi Zhipeng closes a New Year's Day address with it after citing Bodhidharma's five-petaled flower and the seasonal renewal of things.

Senses.Note: Sanyi closes a sermon on one law and many appearances with the pair. Yune uses it to answer gradual versus sudden awakening. Senses.Explanation: Two parts are called different and then placed under one earlier heading. The phrase borrows the language of ordering or classification to settle an exchange without an explanatory comparison. Six current speakers use it to end or redirect different questions, including gradual and sudden awakening.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Eyes meeting eyes
Senses.Note: Asked about the student’s own self, Shiqi replies, “Eyes meeting eyes”; the student’s next question about ending birth and death is treated as starting over. Tian’an says the same when asked what remains after host and guest disappear. Ruibai and Eryin use it for meeting exceptional visitors; Zhufeng answers the intent of the teacher’s arrival from the west, and Dabo answers a question about what remains after mountain and water vanish. Each turns a question about something elsewhere into the meeting already taking place.

Shiqi and Tian’an make the encounter itself answer questions about self and host and guest. Ruibai and Eryin use it for meeting exceptional visitors; Zhufeng and Dabo turn other questions back toward the visible encounter.

Senses.Explanation: Two prizes in one contest names a paired challenge in which two proposed answers or positions meet in one exchange. Shanhui Huan uses the score to answer a New Year question and then tests the cantor's shout. Yezhu Fuhui uses it when asked whether his teaching and the Buddha's are the same or different, then refuses the questioner's celebration. Wumen Huikai places the old fox case's two causality answers side by side and asks why one binds the named master while the other releases him. His next line reverses their order, so the verse keeps the difference between the replies in play.

Senses.Explanation: A double case places a matter under a second case-level demand or joins related public cases for judgment. Yunmen Wenyan takes one problem together under a double charge; Shoushan Xingnian turns a monk's claim of not yet entering the hall into another case; Yuanwu Keqin pairs Zhaozhou Congshen's two hermit encounters; Xuedou Chongxian, Dahui Zonggao, and Yushan Shangsi each use the phrase as a terse verdict. The wording marks case-level doubling, not merely two speakers or propositions.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: Huanglian Yichu answers his interlocutor’s question about how a human king and a teaching king meet by saying that two mirrors illuminate each other and myriad images stand clearly present.

Senses.Explanation: Two mirrors facing each other is an interview image: masters are asked what happens then, and the questioning monk in Xingkong Zhen's assembly supplies it as his own answer before Xingkong rejects it. Yangshan Huiji says two mutually illuminating mirrors have no image between them, and Guishan immediately replies that this claim has already established an image; Zhimen Shouqin answers the same no-image question by telling the questioner to hide the self; Xueyan Zuqin compares Bodhidharma and Emperor Wu’s exchange to mirrors meeting with no gap between them. Huanglian Yichu answers his interlocutor’s question about how a human king and a teaching king meet by saying that two mirrors illuminate each other and myriad images stand clearly present.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB346.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gulin Ru. Gulin calls a monk two-headed and three-faced in his own hall comment on a Xuefeng encounter, then pronounces his own verdict.

Senses.Explanation: Two heads and three faces. The phrase exposes divided, many-faced conduct in direct encounters. Poshan Haiming and Lianyue Daozheng use the expression as direct verdicts in their records; Yuanwu Keqin also gives it directly. Across the three exchanges it labels divided or many-sided conduct rather than supplying a general moral category. Senses.PreferredTarget: Both ends cut off at once; one sword stands cold against the sky

SearchAliases: both ends cut off at once one sword stands cold against the sky
Senses.Note: The line cuts off both sides of a choice and pictures a sword standing cold against the sky. Four recorded masters use it in different settings: a question about earlier and present abbots, a midmonth turning point, a challenge to the division between arising and nonarising, and a question about support in the Linji line. It marks a decisive move that leaves neither side as a safe resting place.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師徵云：「既作臨濟兒孫，須識臨濟綱宗始得。不然，未免傷鋒犯手。或有人問磬山：『語默涉離微，如何通不犯？』豎起拂子云：『見麼？』且道與古人是同是別？不見當時佛鑑老人頌云：『彩雲影裏仙人現，手把紅羅扇遮面。急須著眼看仙人，莫看仙人手中扇。』」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB171.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Tianyin. Tianyin Yuanxiu quotes Fojian Huiqin's verse about an immortal appearing in colored clouds while a red gauze fan covers his face. Its following lines tell the reader to look at the immortal, not the fan. Tianyin first proposes raising his whisk as an answer to a question about speech and silence and asks whether this differs from the old teachers' answers; he then cites the verse. The concrete teaching object is thus also a possible distraction: the listener must examine the one using it. The verse does not authorize inventing a separate invisible being hidden behind every whisk or assuming that merely looking away from the object settles the question.

Even urgently opening one's eyes to look has already fallen into the second position, he says. Fojian remains the cited poet, while Feiyin brings the instruction itself under examination. The warning prevents the reader from turning 'look at the immortal' into another fixed maneuver, as though one could locate a spiritual face by shifting physical attention from fan to holder. Occurrences.Kwic: 四月八日，檀越供法衣，請上堂。師云：「佛佛授手，咸此法衣。彌勒千丈之軀，披來不短；釋迦丈六之身，搭來不長。今日披在寶華身上，耀古騰今，光明赫奕，正偏咸稱，左右逢源，入淨入穢，現土現身，利物應機，辨魔簡異。臨濟道：『我共你入淨玅國土中，著清淨衣說法身佛；入無差別國土中，著無差別衣說報身佛；入解脫國土中，著光明衣說化身佛。』三種國土皆是依變。諸人當知：一切佛法，教則頓漸偏圓、宗則三玄五位，皆是衣，不得在衣上認青、認黃、認赤、認白，須認著衣底人方有入作分。彩雲影裏仙人現，手把紅羅扇遮面，急須著眼看仙人，莫看仙人手中扇。寶華今日將佛衣、法衣一時脫卻，應時即事為諸人露箇消息去也。」良久，云：「𩖼𩖼熏風來入奏，赤條條地我為尊。」下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB300.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chaozong. Receiving an offered religious robe on the Buddha's birthday, Chaozong Tongren quotes Linji's different lands and garments used to teach different Buddha-bodies. All doctrinal divisions and teaching arrangements are clothes, he says: do not merely identify their colors; recognize the wearer. He gives the immortal-and-fan verse and its instruction not to stare at the fan, then says he casts off both Buddha's clothes and teaching clothes to disclose the present matter. After a pause he answers with the warm wind and himself bare. The metaphor directs attention beyond the ceremonial covering without reporting that he physically stripped before the assembly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。「彩雲影裏仙人現，手把紅羅扇遮面。急須著眼看仙人，莫看仙人手中扇。」拂衫袖曰：「者是彩雲影。」揮拂子曰：「者是紅羅扇。作麼生是仙人面？團耶方耶？長耶短耶？紅黃黑白耶？諸仁者！不用看他，只須自看。驀地看破自己面孔，始識儂家面孔。識得儂家面孔，方見仙人面孔。面孔且置，且道適來者一絡索落在什麼處？」震威一喝曰：「霧露雲霞時起滅，長青自古一般天。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB429.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gulin (Prajñā) of Fengtian, Shengjing. Gulin Zhi recites the whole verse, shakes his robe sleeve as the colored cloud and waves his whisk as the red fan. What is the immortal's face: round or square, long or short, or one of the colors? Stop looking at someone else, he says; see one's own face, then his, then the immortal's. He then asks where all that talk falls, shouts and caps it with mist and clouds arising and vanishing against the enduring sky. The current performance recreates the verse to test the assembly, rather than supplying a literal description of an immortal's appearance.

Occurrences.Kwic: 佛果在五祖為元座，有僧請益，風穴語：默涉離微，如何通不犯因緣？偶佛鑑來，果曰：懃兄可為頌出布施他。鑑即頌曰：彩雲影裏仙人現，手把紅羅扇遮面。急須著眼看仙人，莫看仙人手中扇。果深喜之。雪竇道：劈腹剜心又作麼生？萬松道：麤言及細語，皆歸第一義。

Wansong Xingxiu recounts how Yuanwu Keqin, serving as head monk at Wuzu, was asked about Fengxue's speech-and-silence case. When Fojian arrived, Yuanwu asked him to compose a verse for the learner. Fojian produced the cloud, immortal and fan poem, and Yuanwu was pleased. Wansong then places it beside Xuedou's demand to cut open the belly and expose the heart, commenting that rough and refined words alike return to the foremost meaning. This witness explicitly names the poet and the teaching occasion. The quoted apparition is a crafted image answering a case, not a report of an immortal seen by Fojian.

Senses.Explanation: Tianyin Yuanxiu quotes Fojian Huiqin's verse about an immortal appearing in colored clouds while a red gauze fan covers his face. Its following lines tell the reader to look at the immortal, not the fan. Tianyin first proposes raising his whisk as an answer to a question about speech and silence and asks whether this differs from the old teachers' answers; he then cites the verse. The concrete teaching object is thus also a possible distraction: the listener must examine the one using it. The verse does not authorize inventing a separate invisible being hidden behind every whisk or assuming that merely looking away from the object settles the question. Entries.SourceTerm: 彩鳳翻飛身自在，鐵牛奔吼意常閒

Senses.PreferredTarget: A many-colored phoenix wheels freely; an iron ox bellows with its mind at ease.
SearchAliases: A many-colored phoenix wheels freely; an iron ox bellows with its mind at ease
Senses.Note: The impossible animal images describe unrestricted action with untroubled awareness. The pair is poetry within a transmission exchange, not a claim about animals.

Occurrences.Kwic: 關，因閱萬松拈提若面墻者久之，忽一日有省，曰：「此宗非絕後再甦、懸崖撒手者，要望他針線細密，盤旋回互，不觸當頭、兔子搆牛奶，萬萬不可得。」既而幡然出關，參定國從公，得大發明，從撫而印之。拈云：「閱故典有省，古來不無其人。乃復出關參訪，足見此老行已嚴密，不輕自肯，自不可與高亭、玄沙輩同日而語，宜其厚德為洞宗棟梁、法門軌範矣。至如他於定國處得大發明，畢竟發明箇甚麼？若謂本分事，既言本分，豈容他發得明？若不然者，爭又恁麼說？有能於此端的，得許伊承嗣嵩山。」燕京宗鏡院大章宗書禪師燕京宗鏡院大章宗書禪師因廩山忠參，值師外出，山迎而問曰：「達磨面壁石何在？」師指曰：「嗚，那青青黯黯處。」曰：「指東話西作麼？」師曰：「杜撰禪和，如麻似粟。」曰：「者漢在者裏，擬魔魅人那？」師便打。拈云：「廩山當時腳跟若不穩當，幾被者漢賺落青青黯黯底，至今無出頭處。雖然，爭奈到頭遭他屈棒。」西京少室幻休常潤禪師西京少室幻休常潤禪師參小山書公，一日入室呈偈，書把住曰：「子母勦說，更須自入悟門。」師曰：「常不借緣，從何門入？」曰：「既不借緣，何為至此？」師曰：「因不借緣，所以至此。」曰：「就不借緣一語，於意云何？」師曰：「彩鳳翻飛身自在，鐵牛奔吼意常閒。」書遂付以大法。拈云：「少室不借緣則灼然，未免向異類中露出聲跡。」建昌廩山蘊空常忠禪師建昌廩山蘊空常忠禪師受宗鏡付囑，隱從姑山。有顧問者，師但搖手曰：「汝不會我語。」曰：「試說看。」師曰：「南城城外水，滔滔向北流。」問者瞪目。師曰：「向道汝不會我語。」拈云：「廩山倘見顧問者，但瞪目視之，豈特疑殺天下人？亦可使將佛法當等閑不得。」順德蓬鵲山天然圓佐禪師順德蓬鵲山天然圓佐禪師蓬岩吳柱史問：「如何是般若體？」師曰：「寂然不動。」曰：「如何是般若用？」師曰：「感而遂通。」拈云：「蓬山將謂因人說法，善赴來機，不知不唯誤人，而且誤法。何故？若指寂然不動為體，則青山白石何嘗非寂然乎？感而遂通為用，則春鳥夏蟲何嘗非感通乎？要知曹溪波浪如相似，無限平人被陸沉。噓！也是證龜成鱉。」燕京大覺寺慈舟方念禪師燕京大覺寺慈舟方念禪師依少室潤公作維那，一日，遊初祖面壁處，忽然契悟，乃曰：「五乳峰前好箇消息，大小石頭塊塊著地。」呈潤，潤可之。拈云：「大覺恁麼契悟，還諦當也無？若諦當，則未舉游步已前，石頭豈不著地？若不諦當，少室何為印可？於此見得分明，兩父子天然妙絕。」嵩山無言正道禪師嵩山無言正道禪師僧問：「如何是新

Occurrences.Kwic: 璣滿地拋。闌干斜倚，憑誰語，兩岸芙蕖，露滴晚香飄。任公釣錦鰲，釣得錦鰲透碧霄。翻憶西湖，月下弄笙簫，柳鎖長隄十二橋。第三十三祖月舟文載大師掩關，閱《萬松機緣》有省，嘆曰：「洞上宗風大播天下，有織錦回文之功，非鍼線細密，盤旋回互，不觸當頭者，不能與伊作主也。」既而幡然出關，參無方從公，發明己見，撫而印之。春雨山花燦錦，秋風落葉飛金。夜靜幽人得意，猿啼旅客傷心。等閒若不登高朢，爭見東流海漾深？第三十四祖宗鏡宗書大師，聞月舟法席之盛，入室請益，密踐八載，蒙付囑。後少室請師，師慨曰：「先師化後三十餘年，洞上宗風迨乎湮沒。」遂主之，臨終，索筆書偈曰：「宗鏡宗鏡，心法成行。即日圓覺，鏡破宗正。」招手悟猶鈍，那堪八載周？無脣不是兔，有角亦非牛。春信梅花曉，琴聲月下悠。華亭誰更委，翻卻釣魚舟。第三十五祖西京幻休常潤大師參宗鏡，問：「鏡中現像時如何？」曰：「何不打破？」師曰：「其奈鏡像何？」曰：「鏡像安在？」師有省。一日，舉「我今不是渠」，詰之曰：「既不是渠，畢竟是何人？」師曰：「若要識此人，有箇真消息。無相滿虛空，有形沒蹤跡。曾為佛祖師，常作乾坤則。龜毛拂子清風生，兔角杖頭明月出。」鏡復徵之，師曰：「彩鳳翻飛身自在，鐵牛奔吼意常閒。」曰：「善哉。」水潺潺，山疊疊，蹭蹬天涯老劍客。江北江南遍問津，芒鞋蹋綻路頭絕。風吹柳絮走毛毬，雨打梨花飛蛺蝶。乳酪醍醐味不殊，瓶盤釵釧金非別。休休休，直一橛，轉盼家山雲外月。他家父子好機關，說甚臨濟白拈賊。第三十六祖大覺方念大師，參幻休，休問：「甚處來？」師曰：「北方。」曰：「北方道法與此方何如？」師曰：「水分千派，流出一源。」一日，遊初祖面壁處，契悟，乃曰：「五乳峰前，好箇消息，大小石頭，塊塊著地。」詣室呈休，休囑曰：「無上涅槃心，佛祖相傳付。吾今授受時，雲淨峰頭露。」乳峰嶮巇人難到，到者應須膽也銷，紫電光中鳴布鼓，桃花浪裏看騰蛟。頭角昂而機用別，風雲際而意氣豪，遞相承授兮水向源濁，體佛祖心兮霜妒花嬌。眾生末法真堪嘆，艸木皆兵何處逃？第三十七祖雲門圓澂大師掩關，看乾峰「舉一不得舉二」話發明，詣雲棲，棲舉「海底泥牛」，師推出傍僧，曰：「大眾證明。」後參大覺，覺曰：「止風塗向青山近，越王城畔滄海遙時如何？」師曰：「月穿滄海破，波斯不展眉。」復呈偈，覺曰：「語句綿密，不落始終，真當家種艸。向後開兩片皮，截斷天下人舌頭有分在。」一鎚奮力碎重關，直透雷門萬仞山。江練靜，暮雲閒，奪得靈符肘後

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 璣滿地拋。闌干斜倚，憑誰語，兩岸芙蕖，露滴晚香飄。任公釣錦鰲，釣得錦鰲透碧霄。翻憶西湖，月下弄笙簫，柳鎖長隄十二橋。第三十三祖月舟文載大師掩關，閱《萬松機緣》有省，嘆曰：「洞上宗風大播天下，有織錦回文之功，非鍼線細密，盤旋回互，不觸當頭者，不能與伊作主也。」既而幡然出關，參無方從公，發明己見，撫而印之。春雨山花燦錦，秋風落葉飛金。夜靜幽人得意，猿啼旅客傷心。等閒若不登高朢，爭見東流海漾深？第三十四祖宗鏡宗書大師，聞月舟法席之盛，入室請益，密踐八載，蒙付囑。後少室請師，師慨曰：「先師化後三十餘年，洞上宗風迨乎湮沒。」遂主之，臨終，索筆書偈曰：「宗鏡宗鏡，心法成行。即日圓覺，鏡破宗正。」招手悟猶鈍，那堪八載周？無脣不是兔，有角亦非牛。春信梅花曉，琴聲月下悠。華亭誰更委，翻卻釣魚舟。第三十五祖西京幻休常潤大師參宗鏡，問：「鏡中現像時如何？」曰：「何不打破？」師曰：「其奈鏡像何？」曰：「鏡像安在？」師有省。一日，舉「我今不是渠」，詰之曰：「既不是渠，畢竟是何人？」師曰：「若要識此人，有箇真消息。無相滿虛空，有形沒蹤跡。曾為佛祖師，常作乾坤則。龜毛拂子清風生，兔角杖頭明月出。」鏡復徵之，師曰：「彩鳳翻飛身自在，鐵牛奔吼意常閒。」曰：「善哉。」水潺潺，山疊疊，蹭蹬天涯老劍客。江北江南遍問津，芒鞋蹋綻路頭絕。風吹柳絮走毛毬，雨打梨花飛蛺蝶。乳酪醍醐味不殊，瓶盤釵釧金非別。休休休，直一橛，轉盼家山雲外月。他家父子好機關，說甚臨濟白拈賊。第三十六祖大覺方念大師，參幻休，休問：「甚處來？」師曰：「北方。」曰：「北方道法與此方何如？」師曰：「水分千派，流出一源。」一日，遊初祖面壁處，契悟，乃曰：「五乳峰前，好箇消息，大小石頭，塊塊著地。」詣室呈休，休囑曰：「無上涅槃心，佛祖相傳付。吾今授受時，雲淨峰頭露。」乳峰嶮巇人難到，到者應須膽也銷，紫電光中鳴布鼓，桃花浪裏看騰蛟。頭角昂而機用別，風雲際而意氣豪，遞相承授兮水向源濁，體佛祖心兮霜妒花嬌。眾生末法真堪嘆，艸木皆兵何處逃？第三十七祖雲門圓澂大師掩關，看乾峰「舉一不得舉二」話發明，詣雲棲，棲舉「海底泥牛」，師推出傍僧，曰：「大眾證明。」後參大覺，覺曰：「止風塗向青山近，越王城畔滄海遙時如何？」師曰：「月穿滄海破，波斯不展眉。」復呈偈，覺曰：「語句綿密，不落始終，真當家種艸。向後開兩片皮，截斷天下人舌頭有分在。」一鎚奮力碎重關，直透雷門萬仞山。江練靜，暮雲閒，奪得靈符肘後

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 謨定命，扶捄自許，于時言言，于時語語。五乳峰前看月華，皇皇穆穆是誰家？青原第二十九世，西京幻休大千常潤禪師。始閱修多羅，有所警發，後參小山，聞舉洞山「我今不是渠」，師於言下領悟，以偈呈小山曰：「若要識此人，有箇真消息，無相滿虛空，有形沒蹤跡。曾為佛祖師，常作乾坤則，龜毛拂子清風生，兔角杖頭明月出。」山曰：「子母勦說，須自入悟門。」師曰：「當不借緣，從何門入？」山曰：「既不借緣，何為至此？」師曰：「因不借緣，所以至此。」山曰：「就不借緣，於意云何？」師曰：「彩鳳翻飛身自在，鐵牛奔吼意常閒。」山許是克家種艸，即以洞上法印付之，略曰：「定作人天主，當思少室秋。」入海量沙，循山採藻，心志徒勞何日了。一朝撲碎古菱花，妍醜分明都自曉。橫身鬧市邊，垂手撫八埏。杖頭風月本無價，奮肆施為緣不借。少室始基永勿移，新豐振古洵如茲。青原第三十世，燕京大覺寺慈舟方念禪師。參幻休和尚，一見便問：「甚處來？」師曰：「北方。」休曰：「北方道法與此方何如？」師曰：「水分千派，流出一源。」休見其語異，命充堂司。一日，遊初祖面壁處，豁然契悟，曰：「五乳峰前好箇消息，大小石頭塊塊著地。」以偈呈休，遂印可付法。偈曰：「無上涅槃心，佛祖相傳付。吾今授受時，雲淨峰頭露。」時感蕭晨尋哲匠，機觸箭鋒不少讓，乳峰石上連歌唱。

Senses.Explanation: A many-colored phoenix wheels freely; an iron ox bellows with its mind at ease. The impossible animal images describe unrestricted action with untroubled awareness. Huanzhu Changrun speaks the line in the inherited case. Huigong Xiong comments in J35nB336; Baiyu adds a verse in J36nB359; Hansong Cao adds a verse in J37nB392. Zhe’an Fan adds a separate verse after the quoted case in J36nB369. The complete saying and full turn control the sense. The pair is poetry within a transmission exchange, not a claim about animals.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X87/X87n1624.xml). Forest Notes (林間錄). Hong Juefan’s essay cites Shitou’s closing warning in the Cantong qi not to waste one’s time, followed by Fayan Wenyi’s sharp comment “Stop! Stop!” The phrase about kindness being hard to repay comes as Juefan’s appreciation of Fayan’s seeing the earlier teacher’s intent; the next clause speaks of Fayan in the third person. It is a literary judgment on inherited instruction, not Fayan’s own self-reference.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: Fayan’s 注曰 governs 住！住！; the following 恩大難酬 and 法眼可謂... evaluate Fayan in third person. The essay writer Hong Juefan is the present commentator, while Fayan and Shitou are cited figures.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB425.xml). Complete Record of Chan Master Jifei (即非禪師全錄). At the opening of a winter retreat, Jifei Ruyi recalls Miyun Yuanwu’s command that the monks must avoid drowsiness or face a staff blow. Jifei says the old master’s deep concern is a kindness hard to repay, then immediately argues that the warning alone is incomplete: refusing both Chan practice and reflection can cause other errors. He offers a deliberately gentler image of giving a pillow. The thanks are sincere yet paired with a live critique of his predecessor.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB369.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhe’an Fan (蔗菴範禪師語錄). Speaking to donors, Zhe’an Jingfan describes himself wearing out his arm with blows and his mouth with instruction for stubborn monks. He imagines an unnamed unfeeling monk who says his force cannot be restrained and that such kindness is hard to repay, leaving Zhe’an embarrassed; a fanciful visitor then comes at midnight to explain the gift of Dharma. The phrase is voiced by Zhe’an’s imagined monk, not an independent person giving recorded testimony.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: After speaking of stubborn 禪和 monks, Zhe’an says 有不識痛癢漢猶道 before 恩大難酬. This imagined monk voices praise inside Zhe’an’s hall address; no historical person is named.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X81/X81n1568.xml). Strict Lineage of the Five Lamps (Vols. 10–25) (五燈嚴統(第10卷-第25卷)). In a lamp biography of Fozhao Gao, his teacher Yuantong Ji asks what Touzi’s answer means in a case about someone returning from great death. The phrase is Fozhao’s direct response to Ji’s test, not the lamp compiler’s praise.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X84/X84n1583.xml). Orthodox Continuation of the Lamp (續燈正統). The later lamp record presents Wuming Yuanchang raising a case about Langya’s “tree and vine” saying. It quotes Dahui Zonggao calling the exchange a thief’s guilty conscience and then saying, “Even so, a great kindness is hard to repay.” A new “the master said” introduces Wuming’s own assessment, distinguishing Dahui’s quoted concession from Wuming’s current commentary. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (B/B27/B27n0152.xml). Recorded Sayings of National Master Puji Yulin (普濟玉琳國師語錄). At a night assembly, Yulin Tongxiu asks the monks to supply responses to an old case and then challenges their answers as too early or too stiff. After another test about rain, the disciple Xingqi bows and says the master’s kindness is hard to repay; Yulin laughs. The phrase belongs to Xingqi’s response to the immediate teaching, not to Yulin’s own speech.

Senses.Explanation: A great kindness is hard to repay: an expression of gratitude for decisive teaching or help. Hong Juefan uses it while appreciating Fayan’s response to Shitou. Fozhao Gao offers it as the answer to Yuantong Ji’s test; Xingqi says it after Yulin Tongxiu challenges the assembly. Jifei Ruyi praises Miyun’s stern care and then critiques the limit of his warning. Zhe’an Jingfan places the compliment in an imagined disciple’s mouth. A later lamp quotes Dahui using it in the Langya tree-and-vine case before Wuming Yuanchang adds his own assessment. The phrase can therefore be direct thanks, a literary aside or quoted speech.

Senses.PreferredTarget: kindness surpassing that of parents
AlternateTargets: grace exceeding that of one's parents
SearchAliases: grace exceeding that of one's parents
Senses.Explanation: “Kindness surpassing that of parents” is emphatic gratitude for help that enables a person to see for himself. Tianyin Yuanxiu uses it in a substitute reply praising Xuansha's patient pointing. Three independent records preserve Xiangyan saying it of Guishan precisely because Guishan refused to explain and thereby did not deprive him of his own awakening. Juelang Daosheng extends the expression to teachings whose words can enable a reader to enter their meaning.
Senses.Note: The comparison magnifies a teacher's benefit; it does not depreciate parents. In the Xiangyan story, the surpassing kindness is the refusal to supply a second-hand answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不備也。茲者，大師之孫堅如欲募刻師《夢遊全集》，特請為序而贊成之，予嘉其為法忘軀之誠，因述余仰止慕慨之思云爾。紫竹林集序紫竹林集序孔子曰：「辭達而已矣。」教中云：「宗通而後說通。」蓋情見乎辭，不以辭害意，正是意句俱得，宗說皆通也。況文言為載道之器，非文言則道不足以傳。如吾佛祖，皆生西域，滅度之久，孰能知之？亦必籍此言教，始得親見親聞，始知吾人具有，秪因迷悟而差失耳。末法捨此文字言教，又從何而悟入乎？予癸未冬，于金陵會顓大師，相與莫逆，偶別往浙，扶竿徑山。今日重來白門，而師已示寂于紫竹林矣。予深悼而弔之，其室中有千輻、佛地二子，彙師生平法語著作，名《紫竹林集》以請余曰：「此吾師生平之骨髓，師意不欲人序，故闕如也。師獨推重和上，和上俄至，則此感應道交，甚為奇特，末後光明，不待和上發揮之，而誰望乎？」余謂紫竹言教，久信海內，何用更贅？但師之法語著作，皆從胸中流出，稱性而談，所謂言與心親、行與道合，非世人揣摩摹擬之辭翰，與浮言過實者所可比也。有能讀此集，知其意句嚗嚗落處，則亦可從此悟入心性之密，恩逾父母矣。法乳所流，寧有窮哉？重刻證道歌註頌序重刻證道歌註頌序還丹一粒，點銕成金；至理一言，轉凡成聖。此惟吾宗門足以當之，故予嘗令學人熟讀寶誌公《十二時歌》、傅大士《心王銘》、三祖《信心銘》、永嘉《證道歌》、石頭《參同契》、雲巖《寶鏡三昧》諸著作，參研久之，自能隨事觸機，頓入圓明玅性。何則？此諸祖如大醫王，從曠劫來遍採奇異方藥，修煉微玅靈丹，末法之人何幸遇此？如靈丹在口，但能信而吞之，便足起死回生，轉凡成聖，豈非《證道歌》中所謂「粉骨碎身未足酬，一句了然超百億」乎？世人以諸祖無有法嗣，又孰知愈於有法嗣者之法乳益深乎？吾弟子姚愚谷嘗隨予廬山圓通，偶得竺源禪師所註《頌證道歌》，不啻如獲髻珠，深為秘惜。去年攜來金陵，質顓大師贊其梓行，亦自於林中剃落，改號千輻。今復乞予序其流通之意，予曰：「善哉！從上諸祖不吝修證之勞，以自受用者施於末法，而末法自惟將何以報深恩？今子廣為流通，何嘗非析骨刺血之意乎？雖然，莫將容易得，便作等閒看。惟真琉瓶能盛獅乳，其他則裂也。醍醐毒藥，辨之者誰？往往一等癡狂，拾得古人現成

Senses.Explanation: The responsive jewel is a luminous precious object whose displayed color changes with its surroundings. Yongming Yanshou quotes a description in which it shines in darkness, warms or cools, and shows colors in water. Gulin Qingmao’s verse describes its cold light spreading day and night. Liao’an Qingyu raises Yongjia Xuanjue’s inherited jewel verse, while an unnamed monk asks Zihu Lizong about the jewel’s own color. These uses establish a responsive, color-following jewel; they do not themselves define it by wish fulfillment.

Senses.Explanation: People fail to recognize the mani pearl; it is kept close within the Tathagata storehouse. The quoted pearl and storehouse challenge a seeker to identify what cannot be found by grasping an object. Four active Tier-2 deployments by Wanru, Zhuyan Yan, Chulin, and Pufuzhuo. Nanquan turns the search back on the questioner; later masters ask where the pearl is or give their own pointed replies. The pearl and storehouse are images within a Chan exchange, not a physical jewel or container.

Senses.Explanation: The great vehicle is a named body of teaching that Chan masters announce, quote, test, and sometimes declare insufficient. Baizhang Huaihai gives the corpus's direct word-by-word gloss: ‘mahā means great; yāna means vehicle’ (摩訶是大義衍是乘義). Yangshan Huiji announces the great-vehicle teaching from the second seat in his dream, saying that it leaves the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations. Miyun Yuanwu then says Yangshan should have left when invited to speak instead of sounding the block and following the invitation. The term is not merely inherited apparatus. Gusu Zun uses his own ascent of the teaching seat to proclaim it and says everyone has it. Hanyue Fazang then supplies a characteristic Chan check: even the great-vehicle teaching beyond the propositions and negations is ‘good indeed, yet not completely good’ (美則美矣，猶未盡善).

Senses.Explanation: A question asking how to recognize the one who is master amid the crowded world of things and events. Its force lies in putting recognition to the test: the replies point to an immediate act or demand recognition before a verbal answer is formed. In Recorded Sayings of Monk Qianyan, an unnamed monk asks Qianyan Yuanzhang the question during a hall exchange. Qianyan raises a fist. The monk asks what comes after discerning; Qianyan asks where his master is. The raised fist and return question make discerning something the monk must show, rather than a description supplied on his behalf. In Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Hanxiu, an unnamed monk first asks Hanxiu Ruqian for the guest-and-master phrase, then asks how to discern the master amid the vast dust. Hanxiu tells him to recognize it before he has opened his mouth, and the monk bows. This is a distinct present exchange, not a report of Qianyan raising his fist. Compilation of the School Gate's Raising Old Cases preserves an unnamed monk asking Yantou Quanhuo the question; Yantou answers with a copper basin filled with oil. The appended appraisals dispute his adequacy: Tiantong Jie offers the midday sun, while Shishuang Zun proposes a blow across the back. These are later tests of the same old question, not additional monks known by name. Yantou answers the selected turn; he does not utter its question. Hansong Zhicao, in Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Hansong Cao, raises the old question to Yantou and the basin answer at an evening address, then repeats the midday-sun reply and Hongjue Min's passing rider and lifted curtain. He calls each apt, yet says the three have not thoroughly discerned the master amid dust. The selected question is still voiced by the unnamed monk within the raised case; Hansong supplies the present appraisal. Xisou Shaotan, in Expanded Record of Chan Master Xisou Shaotan, directly asks the question in an address thanking the new and former officers. He follows it by saying that one who discerns the master can advance, withdraw, stay, and go as appropriate, then depicts riding Yangqi's three-legged donkey across the directions. Here the challenge belongs to the current address and concerns freedom in handling circumstances, rather than a retelling of Yantou's basin exchange.

Senses.Explanation: The equation of afflictions with awakening is explained through knowing, but its use is sharply restricted: Dahui rejects merely saying it before the matter has been penetrated. The equation reverses the usual opposition between afflictions and awakening, and Chan records both state that reversal and police its recitation. Yuan Cheng answers the direct question by rendering awakening as knowing and perceiving. He says confusion about awakening is called affliction, knowing affliction is awakening, and storing up that knowing is again called affliction. Dahui rebukes people who force the proposition while their conduct contradicts their talk and says only after breaking through may one say it. The Record of Ancient Venerables likewise records beginners claiming a uniform equalized view while their ordinary-and-holy and still-and-noisy distinctions remain twofold. The corpus presents an equation whose repetition masters openly challenge.

Senses.Explanation: ‘Be rain and dew in the sea of affliction, clouds and thunder on the mountain of ignorance’ places effective action inside hard conditions. Masters use its weather images to answer how help, awakening or a staff's force can reach a world still bound up in vexation. Weilin Daopei offers the pair as an alternative to an earlier master's clear-sky answer, then asks whether the two really match. At an ordination, Linye Tongqi uses it to answer what benefiting living beings would be. Baiyu Jingsi asks where a deceased teacher now is and answers with the sea and mountain. Hanxiu Ruqian asks what his staff does after speaking of removing shackles and gives the same images. Hansong Zhicao pictures generations of ancestors acting as rain, dew, cloud and thunder in hard places. Gulin Qingmao uses the pair when asked for one line reaching this side and that, past and present, killing and giving life.

Senses.Explanation: “A mangy horse tethered to a dead stake” is a fixed image for rigid fixation and loss of freedom. Feiyin Tongrong applies it to being bound by verbal schemes and immediately says this leaves no freedom; Yinyuan Longqi independently makes it the result of dead, one-sided fixation. Guxue calls a merely repeated mind-is-Buddha formula a scabby horse tethered to a dead stake. Yuanan applies the scabby-horse image to a frozen use of Buddha preaching in his own fire-opening hall talk.

Senses.Explanation: Sitting securely describes the settled position of a practitioner who truly knows what is at stake. The witness contrasts such an informed monastic, seated at peace, with anyone who has not recognized it and therefore cannot yet claim that stability.

Senses.PreferredTarget: stable, close-set ground

Senses.Explanation: Stable, close-set ground is settled terrain described as secure and intimate; the Chan records place masters and listeners on it and warn against turning it into an achievement. Yuanjie says a predecessor occupied it, Yuanwu describes it as unmoving and cool, Weilin says it exceeds measure and boundary in each person’s share, and Muchen names it within the inherited house style.

Entries.SourceTerm: 蕩蕩一條官驛路，晨昏曾不禁人行

Senses.PreferredTarget: The official post road stretches wide; morning and evening it never bars anyone's passage.
SearchAliases: The official post road stretches wide; morning and evening it never bars anyone's passage.
Senses.Note: Six settings from five work families are retained: Baoning's original verse, Xueyan's two distinct teachings in one family, Feiyin's hall talk, Wanru's critical revoicing and Dugu Chunpeng's sermon. X83 explicitly heads the last teacher Dugu Chunpeng of Lingyin; Tianning is his local seat reference, not a different proved person. He remains source-named unlinked. X66 repeats Baoning or Xueyan, and X79 repeats the original verse, so those copies remain reserves. No global exhaustion is claimed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 見佛來。我佛親見賓頭盧，眉長髮短雙目麤。阿育王，猶疑狐。唵嚤呢噠哩㗭哩囌嚧。梁武帝問達磨：如何是聖諦第一義？磨云：廓然無聖。帝云：對朕者誰？磨云：不識。燒得通紅打一鎚，周遭無數火星飛。十成好箇金剛鑽，攤向門前賣與誰。達磨一日云：吾住世非久，誰得吾正宗者出來與汝證明？道副云：如我所見，不執文字，不離文字，以為道用。磨云：汝得吾皮。尼總持云：我今所解，如慶喜觀阿閦佛國，一見更不再見。磨云：汝得吾肉。道育云：四大本空，五陰非有，而我見處實無一法可當情。磨云：汝得吾骨。二祖出，禮三拜，依位而立。磨云：汝得吾髓。門前諸子列成行，各逞英雄越霸王。如何獨有無言者，坐斷毗盧不可當。六祖見二僧爭風幡，一云：風動。一云：幡動。祖云：不是風動，不是幡動。蕩蕩一條官驛路，晨昏曾不禁人行。渾家不是不進步，無柰當門荊棘生。六祖問讓：和尚甚處來？讓云：嵩山。祖云：什麼物恁麼來？讓云：說似一物即不中。祖云：還假修證不？讓云：修證即不無，汙染即不得。祖云：即此不汙染，是諸佛所護念。吾亦如是，汝亦如是，西天二十七祖般若多羅讖汝後出一馬駒，踏殺天下人去在。戴角披毛恁麼來，鐵圍山嶽盡衝開，閻浮踏殺人無數，驀鼻深穿拽不回。法華經云：大通智勝佛，十劫坐道場，佛法不現前，不得成佛道。三際斷時凡聖盡，十身圓處剎塵周。無私應物隨高下，末過僧祇大劫修。維摩云：其施汝者，不名福田；供養汝者，墮三惡道。無邊無際休斟酌，潮去潮來本自平。清濁淺深并苦淡，一般滋味迥分明。金剛經云：一切賢聖皆以無為法而有差別。仁者見之謂之仁，智者見之謂之智。寒時向火熱
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1350.xml). In Baoning Renyong's own verse sequence, the source raises Huineng encountering the monks' dispute over whether wind or banner moves. Baoning's following verse opens with the selected official-road couplet, then says the household is indeed trying to advance but thorns have grown at the door. The quoted case and new four-line verse make this the direct original verse witness. Huineng speaks in the preceding encounter, while Baoning authors the road image used to appraise it.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1397.xml). At winter-solstice small assembly, Xueyan Zuqin raises Jinfeng asking how a monk passed his checkpoint and then claiming nobody can pass it. Xueyan says passing requires an eye that penetrates the barrier and guarding requires someone able to hold it, yet finds that Jinfeng was caught napping by the monk. He closes with the selected road image. Xueyan directly revoices the pair here to judge this different encounter, rather than merely quoting Baoning's wind-banner verse.

Occurrences.Kwic: 遮僧如何？不是風動，不是幡動，甚處見祖師？天目下語：是風動？是幡動？遮僧如何？貪觀白浪，失却手橈。不是風動，不是幡動，甚處見祖師？揭却腦葢。佛照喜之。後到松源會下，因舉前話，松源乃橫點頭。且道是不肯佛照如此舉話耶？是不肯天目如此下語耶？汝等諸人若於橫點頭處見得祖師，識破二僧，便見法昌遇和尚頌云：不是風兮不是幡，黑花猫子面門斑。夜行人只貪明月，不覺和衣渡水寒。畢竟遮一頌意作麼生？只如道：不是風兮不是幡，黑花猫子面門斑。却落在什麼處？後面又道：夜行人只貪明月，不覺和衣渡水寒。又作麼生？如今有一等在情識意路上行底，未免道是頌，二僧只知是風動，是幡動，却不知是心動。若果如是，法昌堪作什麼？當知道他古人著著自有出身之路。豈不見保寧勇和尚頌云：蕩蕩一條官驛路，晨昏曾不禁人行。渾家不是不進步，無奈當門荊棘生。不妨說得太煞明白。山僧今日舉也舉了，注也注了，只是要見祖師與二僧大遠在。聽取一頌：兩岸桃花紅欲然，洞中流出自涓涓。仙家不會論春夏，石爛松枯是一年。上堂：依依稀稀，彷彷彿彿，名不得，狀不得，三世諸佛於此沒溺深坑，帶累天下老和尚與盡大地衲子總跳不出。試舉看。南岳讓和尚往曹溪參六祖，棄却衣下明珠，却向外邊尋逐。祖問：甚處來曲開方便？讓曰：嵩山來道途䟦涉。曰：什麼物恁麼來？無端！無端！讓曰：說似一物即不中，大好！大好！祖曰：還假修證也無？探竿影草。讓曰：修證即不無，染汙即不得，添得一重狼籍。祖曰：即此不染汙，諸佛之所護念。汝既如是，吾亦如是。冬瓜印子。然雖如是，自古自今撐天拄地、戴角擎頭者如稻麻竹葦，要且未
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1397.xml). In a separate extended discussion of the wind-banner encounter and later teachers' readings, Xueyan explicitly quotes Baoning's complete verse. He says it speaks plainly enough but that his own raising and annotation still stand far from seeing the ancestor and the two monks. He then supplies a fresh verse about peach blossoms, a flowing cave stream and an immortal's unmeasured year. Baoning voices the selected couplet within this quotation; Xueyan supplies the present interpretive challenge. This and the checkpoint teaching are distinct settings in one work family.

Later teachers use the opening pair to assess a guarded pass, test interpretations of the wind and banner, affirm the shared ground of ordinary and holy, or offer a different route through a teaching. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X87/X87n1624.xml). Forest Notes. Huihong's Forest Notes narrates that Changsha Jingcen touched a dead monk, told the assembly that the monk raised a real question, and gave this verse. The diamond body is neither false nor true in its final couplet. Huihong transmits Changsha's own funeral verse and then compares further sayings about deceased monks.

Senses.Explanation: Changsha's funeral verse refuses to turn the body of awakening into either a false object or a fixed true object, and later commentators use the paradox to discuss death and perception. Huihong preserves Changsha Jingcen's verse spoken while touching a deceased monk. Linquan Conglun quotes that record in an old-case commentary and adds his own remark about cutting off both sides. Yongjue Yuanxian cites the line in a separate sermon, explaining Changsha's diamond body from the absence of seeing and hearing before expanding to another teacher's saying. These are one original funeral verse and two distinct interpretive deployments.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Senses.Explanation: Xiyuan turns his two shouted verdicts of 'wrong' back on Tianping, asking who owns the errors rather than explaining either verdict. Tianping Congyi boasts that no one can raise a case with him. Xiyuan calls his name; Tianping looks up and moves closer, and Xiyuan calls each response wrong. He then asks whether those two errors are his own or Tianping's. Tianping accepts the blame, only to hear another 'wrong.' The original encounter survives here in a useful lamp witness. Tianyin diagnoses Tianping's confident travel and offers a sharper retort; Lingrui Ni gives a verse; Chaozong Huifang says Tianping fell into Xiyuan's trap; Tianqi's verse comments on the missed point. Each later treatment quotes Xiyuan's question without taking over its utterance.
